explanations.answer: Jesus heals him so he can speak and see
explanations.explanation: Right there in front of everybody, Jesus heals the man so that he can speak and see. Two problems, one healing, no waiting. I think that man's first look at the crowd must have been something. Imagine being able to see and speak in the same moment.

explanations.answer: Jesus sends him to the temple priests
explanations.explanation: The text never sends this man anywhere. Jesus heals him so that he can speak and see. The healing comes straight from Jesus, with no one else in between.

explanations.answer: Jesus sends him to wash in a pool
explanations.explanation: That's a different healing, where Jesus tells a blind man to wash in the pool of Siloam (John 9:7). Here, Jesus just heals him so that he can speak and see. The text doesn't mention any trip.

explanations.answer: If He could be the Son of David
explanations.explanation: The crowds were astounded and asked, "Could this be the Son of David?" They saw a man healed so that he could speak and see, and a big question came out of their mouths. Notice it's a question, not an announcement. I think they were still picking their jaws up off the floor.

explanations.answer: If He could be Elijah come back
explanations.explanation: Elijah, the prophet (1 Kings 18:36), isn't who the crowds name here. They ask, "Could this be the Son of David?" That's the question that comes out of them after the healing. I think they were too astounded to read from anybody else's script.

explanations.answer: If He could be John the Baptist
explanations.explanation: John the Baptist, who came preaching in the Desert of Judea (Matthew 3:1), isn't the name the crowds bring up here. What they ask is, "Could this be the Son of David?" That's the whole question. I think when you're that astounded, you don't have time for a long guessing list.

Not quite, baker. The Pharisees, strict religious leaders, say the opposite. They say, "Only by Beelzebul, the prince of demons, does this man drive out demons." So they point to the prince of demons, not to God. Jesus is about to answer that, and He doesn't hold back.

You've got it, baker. The Pharisees, strict religious leaders, say, "Only by Beelzebul, the prince of demons, does this man drive out demons." The crowds were wondering about the Son of David, and these leaders went a totally different direction. Same healing, two very different reactions.

Jesus says, "Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste…" A kingdom that fights itself is in real trouble. I've seen two cookie cutters argue over the same spot on the dough, and nobody wins that one. Jesus adds that the same goes for any city or household.
Jesus says the opposite. "Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste…" Being split in two doesn't double anything. It just breaks the kingdom apart.

That's not what Jesus says. He says, "Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste…" And He adds that a city or household divided against itself will not stand. A divided kingdom isn't built for the long haul.

Jesus asks, "If Satan drives out Satan, he is divided against himself. How then can his kingdom stand?" His point is that a kingdom pulling against itself can't hold together. It's like a team where everybody pushes the other way.

Jesus doesn't say anything about demons listening. He says, "If Satan drives out Satan, he is divided against himself. How then can his kingdom stand?" The trouble He names is a kingdom that can't stand. I think that's plenty of trouble already.

Jesus doesn't talk about power running out here. He says that if Satan drives out Satan, he is divided against himself, and then asks, "How then can his kingdom stand?" The problem is the division, and a divided kingdom can't stand.

Jesus says, "So then, they will be your judges." He asks the Pharisees by whom their own sons drive out demons, if He does it by Beelzebul. Those sons are the Pharisees' own, and Jesus puts them right in the middle of the question. I'd feel that one all the way down to my gold base.
Jesus doesn't call them followers. He says, "So then, they will be your judges." These are the Pharisees' own sons, who drive out demons too. Judges is the word He picks.

Close, but Jesus uses a different word. He says, "So then, they will be your judges." The Pharisees' own sons drive out demons, so Jesus puts that question right back on them. Judges is the word He picks.

Yes, baker. Jesus says, "But if I drive out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you." That's the other option, set right beside the Pharisees' claim. Two choices, and He says what the second one means.

This one is true, baker. Jesus says, "But if I drive out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you." He puts it right after asking about Beelzebul. So He names what it means if the power is from the Spirit of God.

Jesus says no one can plunder a strong man's house "…unless he first ties up the strong man?" Only then can he plunder the house. First the strong man, then the house. Order matters, same as dough before oven.

Jesus doesn't mention paying anybody off. He says you can't plunder a strong man's house "…unless he first ties up the strong man?" The strong man has to be tied up first. After that, the house can be plundered.
Sneaking sounds smart, but it's not in Jesus' picture. He says nobody can plunder the house "…unless he first ties up the strong man?" Tying him up comes first. Then he can plunder his house.
Jesus says, "He who is not with Me is against Me…" There's no middle seat in that sentence. It's said plainly, and you can't miss it.

Jesus says, "…he who does not gather with Me scatters." Gathering and scattering are opposites, and He puts them side by side. Think of crumbs: gather them up or they go everywhere. I've swept up plenty of those.
Behind isn't the word Jesus uses. He says, "He who is not with Me is against Me…" The word that fills that blank is against.
Jesus doesn't say anyone waits in this line. He says, "…he who does not gather with Me scatters." Not gathering turns into scattering. Waiting isn't on the menu.
Resting sounds nice, but it's not Jesus' word here. He says, "…he who does not gather with Me scatters." The word that closes the line is scatters. Nobody gets a nap in that sentence.

Jesus says, "…every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven men, but the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven." That's a heavy line. Notice how wide the first half is: every sin and blasphemy. Only this one is named as the exception.

The temple isn't what Jesus names. He says every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven men, "…but the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven." The one exception is blasphemy against the Spirit. It's a heavy line, so it's good to read it carefully.

That's not the one Jesus names. He says, "…every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven men, but the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven." The exception is the Spirit, not the Law. It's a heavy teaching, so let's keep it just as He said it.

Careful, baker, because it's the other way around. Jesus says, "Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven…" The one that will not be forgiven is speaking against the Holy Spirit. That's an easy pair to mix up.

That's right, baker. Jesus says, "Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven…" He then says whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven. Two different lines, and He keeps them apart.
Jesus says, "…a tree is known by its fruit." You don't judge a tree by how it looks from far away. You look at what it makes. Same as my cookies: the proof is in the batch.

explanations.answer: By the roots it puts down
explanations.explanation: Roots are out of sight, and Jesus doesn't point to them. He says, "…a tree is known by its fruit." The fruit is what shows you. Roots stay underground, so you'd be digging all day.
Tall is impressive, but it's not what Jesus names. He says, "…a tree is known by its fruit." Height doesn't make the list. The fruit does the talking.
Jesus says, "…out of the overflow of the heart the mouth speaks." Think of a bowl filled right to the top. What's inside spills out the sides. The mouth just shows what's already in there.
Jesus doesn't say home. He says, "…out of the overflow of the heart the mouth speaks." So the words come from what fills the heart. Home isn't the source He names.

Jesus doesn't point to the crowd here. He says, "…out of the overflow of the heart the mouth speaks." The words come out of the heart. A crowd can be loud, but He's talking about what's inside a person.

Yes, baker. Jesus says, "…the evil man brings evil things out of his evil store of treasure." Right before that, He says the good man brings good things out of his good store. A person brings out what's stored up. That's a good reminder to watch what we pack in.

This one is true, baker. Jesus says, "…the evil man brings evil things out of his evil store of treasure." He says it right after saying the good man brings good things out of his good store. Two stores, and each one brings out its own kind.

Jesus says, "…men will give an account on the day of judgment for every careless word they have spoken." Every careless word, not just the big speeches. I talk a lot, so I'm taking that one seriously.

Careful is the opposite of what Jesus says. He says, "…every careless word they have spoken." It's the careless words that men will give an account for. The words we toss out without thinking count too.
Rehearsed is an interesting guess, but it's not the word Jesus uses. He says, "…every careless word they have spoken." Careless is the word He names for the words men will give an account for.

Jesus says, "…by your words you will be acquitted, and by your words you will be condemned." Acquitted means cleared. Our words matter either way. That's a good reason to be thoughtful about what comes out.
Jesus doesn't say ignored. He says, "…by your words you will be acquitted, and by your words you will be condemned." Both outcomes come from words. Nothing here gets ignored.

Remembered isn't the word Jesus uses. He says, "…by your words you will be acquitted, and by your words you will be condemned." Acquitted is the first one, and it's set against condemned. Words carry real weight in this line.
